description: Fallacies about how evidence is gathered and used, and the cognitive biases beneath many fallacies, each in four layers.

depth.picture: Fallacies about the quality of the evidence itself: too little of it, chosen selectively, or misread.
depth.mechanism: The argument uses data that is unrepresentative, cherry-picked, or wrongly interpreted, so the conclusion looks more strongly supported than the evidence really allows.
depth.detail: Members include hasty generalization, anecdotal evidence, cherry picking, survivorship bias, the Texas sharpshooter, the gambler's fallacy, the base rate fallacy, and composition and division. Questions to ask about any statistic: how many cases? how were they chosen? what is missing? compared with what? Most of these come down to whether the sample and the comparison are fair.
depth.principles: Evidence is only as good as the process that produced it. The same numbers can support opposite conclusions depending on what was counted and what was left out, which is why the method matters as much as the result.

depth.picture: Drawing a broad conclusion from a handful of cases.
depth.mechanism: You see a few examples, notice what they have in common, and assume it holds for the whole group. The sample is too small or too unrepresentative to justify it.
depth.detail: Example: two rude waiters, so the whole city is unfriendly. It is a failure of induction: the strength of a generalization depends on sample size and on how the sample was chosen. Stereotypes are often built this way. A good habit is to ask how many cases the claim rests on, how they were selected, and whether there are counterexamples I have not seen.
depth.principles: Small samples are noisy, and vivid ones are misleading. A generalization is only as reliable as the fairness and size of the sample behind it, which is what statistics measures and intuition tends to ignore.

depth.picture: Treating a personal story as proof.
depth.mechanism: A single memorable case is offered as if it settled a general question. It is vivid and personal, so it feels weightier than numbers, though it is only one data point.
depth.detail: My grandfather smoked two packs a day and lived to ninety. Anecdotes are useful for generating ideas and illustrating a finding, but they suffer from selection (the stories we hear are the striking ones), from memory distortion, and from no comparison group. Population data can handle what one case cannot: how often, and compared with what.
depth.principles: One case cannot tell you a rate. Rates require counting all cases, the uneventful ones included, and the human mind remembers and repeats the exceptions, which makes stories a poor guide to how common things are.

depth.picture: Showing only the evidence that supports your case and leaving out the rest.
depth.mechanism: From a mixed body of evidence you select what fits, and present it as if it were the whole. Each fact may be true; the picture they form is false because of what was omitted.
depth.detail: Examples: quoting the one study that found an effect and ignoring twenty that did not; choosing a start date for a chart that makes a trend look better; citing a single hot day as evidence against climate trends, or a single cold one. Defenses: look for systematic reviews, ask what is missing, and check whether the choice of range or examples was principled or convenient.
depth.principles: Given enough data, some subset will say almost anything. Honest use of evidence means reporting the whole body, or explaining why the selection is fair, since selection is itself a way of arguing.

depth.picture: Studying only what survived, and missing what did not.
depth.mechanism: A filter removes the failures before you look. What remains seems typical, so you draw lessons from the winners without seeing that the losers did the same things.
depth.detail: The classic example: in the Second World War, analysts proposed armoring the parts of returning bombers that showed the most bullet holes. Abraham Wald pointed out that those were the places planes could be hit and still return; the planes hit elsewhere did not come back. Business advice drawn only from successful companies is a common modern case. The fix is to look for the missing cases.
depth.principles: Data is a product of a selection process, and what is invisible can matter more than what is visible. Asking what is not in the sample, and why, is one of the most useful habits in reasoning about evidence.

depth.picture: Shooting at a barn wall, then painting a target around the tightest cluster of holes.
depth.mechanism: You look at the data, find a pattern after the fact, and then treat it as if it had been predicted. Random data always contains clusters, so any pattern found this way is unimpressive.
depth.detail: Example: finding that cancer cases cluster in one neighborhood, then drawing the boundary tightly around them and blaming a local cause. With many places and many diseases, some clusters will occur by chance. Statisticians guard against it by specifying a hypothesis in advance, correcting for the number of comparisons made, and testing on new data.
depth.principles: Human beings are pattern detectors, and noise is full of patterns. The test of a real pattern is whether it predicts something not yet seen, which is why forecasts made in advance count for more than explanations fitted afterward.

depth.picture: Believing that after a run of one outcome, the opposite is due.
depth.mechanism: You think random events must balance out in the short run, so after five heads a tail feels overdue. But independent events have no memory.
depth.detail: A fair coin has a fifty percent chance of heads on every flip, whatever came before. The law of large numbers says the proportion evens out over very many trials, not that the next one compensates; the run simply gets diluted. Famous case: at a Monte Carlo casino in 1913 the roulette ball fell on black twenty-six times in a row, and players lost fortunes betting on red. Related is the hot-hand fallacy, its mirror image.
depth.principles: Independence means the past carries no information about the next trial. Intuition expects randomness to look mixed and balanced even in short sequences, but true randomness contains streaks.

depth.picture: Ignoring how common something is when judging what a test result means.
depth.mechanism: A test that is quite accurate can still give mostly false alarms if the thing it looks for is rare. Most people who test positive are then healthy, because healthy people vastly outnumber the sick.
depth.detail: Suppose a disease affects 1 in 1,000 people and a test is 99 percent accurate both ways. In 100,000 people, 100 are sick and 99 test positive; of the 99,900 healthy people, about 999 test positive. So of roughly 1,098 positives, only 99, about 9 percent, are truly sick. Bayes' theorem formalizes this: the answer depends on the prior probability as well as the test.
depth.principles: Evidence should update a prior belief, not replace it. Ignoring how likely something was to begin with is why people misjudge medical tests, security screening, and forensic matches, and why rare events need far stronger evidence than common ones.

depth.picture: Assuming what is true of the parts is true of the whole, or the reverse.
depth.mechanism: You move a property between levels without justification. Every part has it, so the whole must; or the whole has it, so each part must.
depth.detail: Composition: every player on the team is excellent, so the team is excellent (teamwork may be poor). Division: the company is profitable, so every department is. Some properties do carry over (weight adds up) and others do not (a crowd can be noisy without any person being loud). Emergent properties are cases where the whole has features the parts do not, such as wetness or intelligence.
depth.principles: Systems have properties that arise from organization, not just from the parts. Whether a feature transfers between levels depends on the feature, and that has to be checked, not assumed.

depth.picture: Predictable quirks in how minds judge, remember, and decide.
depth.mechanism: The brain uses shortcuts (heuristics) to decide quickly with limited information. They usually work, and in certain situations they lead to systematic, repeatable errors.
depth.detail: Researchers, notably Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, have catalogued dozens: anchoring, availability, confirmation bias, hindsight bias, framing, sunk cost, and more. They arise from limited attention, from emotion, and from mental efficiency. Awareness helps only somewhat; better protection comes from process: checklists, base rates, seeking disconfirming views, and deciding in advance what would change your mind.
depth.principles: Bias is not stupidity. It is the price of thinking fast in a complicated world, and it affects experts as well as amateurs. The remedy is to build habits and structures that compensate, since intelligence alone does not remove it.

depth.picture: Looking for, noticing, and remembering what agrees with what you already think.
depth.mechanism: Once you hold a belief, you search for support, interpret ambiguous evidence in its favor, and forget or discount what conflicts. You feel fair throughout.
depth.detail: Peter Wason's 2-4-6 task showed it: people given the number sequence 2, 4, 6 and asked to find the rule tended to test only sequences that fit their guess, never ones that might break it. Online, algorithms that show what we already like reinforce it. Countermeasures: actively seek disconfirming evidence, state what would change your mind, and ask someone to argue the other side.
depth.principles: A belief that is only ever tested against confirming cases can never be corrected. The asymmetry between confirming and refuting, a single counterexample can refute what many confirmations cannot prove, is why looking for failure is the more informative test.

depth.picture: Leaning too heavily on the first number or idea you hear.
depth.mechanism: An initial value, even an arbitrary one, becomes a reference point. Later estimates are adjusted from it, usually not far enough.
depth.detail: In a well-known experiment, people spun a wheel of fortune that landed on 10 or 65, then estimated the share of African countries in the United Nations; the estimates followed the random number. Negotiators use it by naming a price first; sellers show a high original price beside the discount. Defenses: form your own estimate before hearing others', and consider the range of possible values.
depth.principles: The mind estimates by adjusting from a starting point, and the adjustment is typically insufficient. Any number in the environment, relevant or not, can become that starting point, which is why the first offer has outsized influence.

depth.picture: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.
depth.mechanism: Vivid, recent, or emotional events are easy to recall, so they feel common. Ordinary events are less memorable, so they feel rare.
depth.detail: People overestimate deaths from plane crashes, shark attacks, and terrorism, which get heavy news coverage, and underestimate deaths from heart disease and falls. A fresh news story can change perceived risk overnight. To correct it, look at actual frequencies from data rather than at what comes to mind, and notice how media choice shapes memory.
depth.principles: Ease of recall is a decent cue to frequency when experience is a fair sample, and a poor one when the sample is filtered by drama. Memory and media both favor the unusual, so the world feels more dangerous and strange than it is.

depth.picture: Carrying on with something because of what has already been spent.
depth.mechanism: Money, time, or effort already invested feels like a reason to keep going. But it is gone either way, and only future costs and benefits should count.
depth.detail: Examples: sitting through a bad film because you paid for the ticket; continuing a failing project because so much has gone into it; staying in a poor relationship for the years already spent. The rational rule is to compare from now on: what is the future value of continuing against stopping? Loss aversion and the wish to avoid admitting a mistake make it hard to apply.
depth.principles: Decisions are about the future, and the past cannot be changed by them. Sunk costs matter emotionally, since we dislike waste, but treating them as reasons compounds the loss.

depth.picture: After the fact, feeling that it was obvious all along.
depth.mechanism: Once you know an outcome, your memory of what you expected shifts toward it. The past seems more predictable than it really was.
depth.detail: Baruch Fischhoff showed it in the 1970s: people asked to estimate the likelihood of events beforehand, and later to recall their estimates, remembered giving higher probabilities to what actually happened. It makes decision-makers seem foolish for missing signs that were only clear afterward, and it makes us overconfident about future prediction. A partial cure is to write down predictions and reasons before the outcome.
depth.principles: Knowledge of the result contaminates memory of the uncertainty. To judge a decision fairly, ask what could have been known at the time and how the odds looked then, not how things turned out.

depth.picture: Reasoning your way toward the conclusion you want.
depth.mechanism: When we care about an outcome, we scrutinize unwelcome evidence harshly and accept welcome evidence easily, while feeling fair the whole time.
depth.detail: Researchers find that people with strong political or personal commitments evaluate the same study differently depending on whether it supports them, and that greater intelligence can make it worse, since more skill means better rationalizations. Signs: applying different standards to friendly and unfriendly evidence, and asking can I believe this? versus must I believe this? Approaches that help include precommitting to standards and considering how you would judge the evidence if the conclusion were reversed.
depth.principles: Reasoning is often a lawyer working for a client, not a judge. Recognizing that our conclusions can be shaped by what we hope is true is a first step toward balancing it, especially on subjects tied to identity.

depth.picture: The same facts feel different depending on how they are put.
depth.mechanism: Wording that highlights gains or losses, or survival or death, changes which option feels better even though the information is identical.
depth.detail: Tversky and Kahneman's disease problem: a treatment that saves 200 of 600 people is preferred to one with a one-third chance of saving all, but when the same outcomes are framed as 400 people will die, the preference reverses. Ground beef labeled 75 percent lean sells better than 25 percent fat. Defense: restate the problem in different terms and see whether your answer changes.
depth.principles: People do not evaluate options in the abstract; they evaluate a description of them. Because wording is a choice, whoever frames a question has real influence, and noticing the frame is the first step to reasoning about what is underneath.

depth.picture: People with little skill in an area tend to overrate their ability in it.
depth.mechanism: The knowledge needed to do something well is the same knowledge needed to recognize good performance. Without the first, the second is missing too, so the unskilled cannot see how far they are from competent.
depth.detail: From a 1999 study by Justin Kruger and David Dunning, in which the lowest scorers on tests of logic and grammar rated themselves well above average. Later work suggests part of the pattern arises from regression to the mean and general overestimation, so the size of the effect is debated. The durable lesson is modest: confidence is a poor guide to competence, and experts also underestimate how much they know.
depth.principles: Self-assessment depends on skill. Feedback, calibration training, and comparison with objective measures help, and humility is more reasonable when one is a beginner: not knowing what you do not know is a hazard for everyone.
